analysis.one_liner: Moves the consumer financial watchdog from independent Fed funding to yearly congressional appropriations.
analysis.headline: The bill to switch the CFPB to annual appropriations was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau writes and enforces rules against banks, lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting companies. Under current law it does not depend on the yearly spending bills Congress passes; it draws its budget from the Federal Reserve. This bill would end that arrangement and make the bureau depend on an annual appropriation starting in fiscal 2023, giving Congress the power to shrink or cut off its budget each year. It would also limit the bureau's use of civil penalty money to direct victim payments, sending any leftover penalty funds to the Treasury.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, payday and installment lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting companies — the firms the CFPB polices — would gain, because a bureau funded through annual appropriations can be squeezed each year through the spending process. Approps champions in Congress would also gain a lever over an agency that currently sets its own budget request.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the CFPB's current funding source — transfers from the Federal Reserve outside the annual appropriations process — and replaces it with money Congress must approve each year [S2][S3].
It directs any civil penalty money left in the fund after victims are paid to the Treasury general fund, rather than remaining available to the bureau [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the cost: a consumer watchdog whose budget can be cut in the annual spending process is easier to defund or slow down, and the industries it polices would face weaker oversight. The agency's enforcement and rulemaking pace would depend on yearly congressional budget fights rather than its own assessment of its workload.

drawbacks.text: The strongest case for the bill: the CFPB is one of the few federal regulators whose funding does not go through Congress at all, and supporters argue annual appropriations are the ordinary way to hold a powerful agency accountable to elected representatives [S2][S3].

An honest opponent would concede that Congress has a legitimate interest in overseeing agency budgets; the disagreement is that an appropriations constraint on this particular regulator functions in practice as a lever for the industries being regulated to shrink enforcement through the yearly spending process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is sincere and the agency's off-budget funding is genuinely unusual. But the practical effect is to place the main consumer finance regulator's survival in the annual spending process, where financial industry lobbying is strongest and where a funding cutoff requires no public vote on any consumer protection rule. The accountability gained is general; the enforcement capacity put at risk is specific and substantial.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee never took the bill up after referral, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Hagerty introduced the bill on September 21, 2021 [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day; no committee or floor action followed [S5].
Twenty-four Republican senators cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill never received a vote and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers came out ahead: the CFPB's independent funding structure survived, leaving the financial firms it polices with no new lever to shrink its budget through the yearly spending process.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers; the CFPB kept independent funding

for.name: Sen. Bill Hagerty
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to subject the CFPB to annual appropriations.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Sherrod Brown, D)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on the bill after referral; it sat with no action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support, and the Democratic-led Banking Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The CFPB polices these firms' fees, lending, and servicing practices; moving its funding into the annual appropriations process would give their congressional allies a yearly opportunity to cut its budget. Their gain would come at the cost of weaker enforcement for consumers.

industries.industry: Payday lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting agencies
industries.note: These are among the most frequent targets of CFPB enforcement actions. A bureau dependent on annual appropriations would be easier to weaken, reducing the risk of penalties and new rules against these industries.
